title: Concept model B: climate models and their uncertainty
subject: science
phenomenonOrContext: A climate model reproduces an observed warming trend within a stated uncertainty range, then produces different future ranges under different emissions scenarios.
lessonGoal: Evaluate climate-model evidence by separating validation, physical uncertainty, scenario assumptions, and unsupported certainty.
successCriteria: I compare observations with a modeled range rather than one exact line.
I distinguish uncertainty in the physical response from uncertainty in future human choices.
I make a bounded claim supported by data and model structure.
I identify a limitation and evidence that would strengthen the evaluation.

vocabulary.definition: a model run for a past period that can be compared with observations
a stated set of possible future conditions or choices used as model input
an interval representing quantified limits from data, parameters, model structure, or variability
a conditional model result under stated assumptions, not an unconditional prediction

sections.title: NOTICE — Test the model on past conditions
sections.body: A fictional climate-model evaluation uses temperature anomaly relative to its own baseline. The model was run without fitting to the final three evaluation points.

data.provenance: Manuel Academy fictional evaluation dataset constructed to teach model validation. Values are not historical climate observations or a published projection.
data.limit: Three aggregate points cannot evaluate regional extremes, ocean heat, precipitation, or every feedback.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by this evaluation table?

choices.label: The observations fall within the modeled ranges for these three aggregate periods.
The model has proved every regional climate outcome exactly.
Any uncertainty range means the model provides no information.

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Match claim scale to evidence scale
sections.body: Agreement at three aggregate points is evidence that the model captures the tested trend within its stated range. It does not validate every variable, region, feedback, or future scenario. A quantified range still carries information and should not be treated as ignorance.

sections.title: LEARN — Three sources of spread
sections.body: Climate models encode physical laws and are evaluated against past and present observations. Internal variability creates different short-term paths even with the same forcing. Parameter and structural uncertainty create a range of physical responses. Scenario uncertainty comes from conditional future choices such as emissions. These sources should be separated because better observations can narrow some ranges, while a future human choice is not a measurement error.

sequence: physical laws plus boundary conditions plus forcing inputs
comparison with observations across multiple variables and scales
reference.feedbackLoop: Evaluation can revise model structure or parameter estimates before projection.
reference.readingRule: The sequence and labels carry meaning without color.

sections.title: MODEL — Compare scenario ranges without false precision
sections.body: The fictional model projects a 2081–2100 anomaly of 1.1–1.6 °C under Scenario L and 2.0–2.9 °C under Scenario H, relative to its baseline.

items.prompt: Model task: state a defensible comparison.

steps: Identify the conditional inputs: Scenario L and Scenario H are different assumed futures.
Compare intervals, not just midpoints: the entire H range is above the entire L range in this fictional run.
Claim that higher forcing in Scenario H produces a higher projected anomaly range in this model.
Do not claim an exact 2100 temperature or assign a probability to the human choice of scenario unless the source provides one.
Limit the result to the stated model, variable, period, baseline, and scenario definitions.

sections.title: YOUR TURN — Separate uncertainty types
sections.body: A report says: The model range is wide because scientists do not know whether society will follow Scenario L or H, and because clouds respond identically in every model.

items.prompt: Revise the report to distinguish scenario uncertainty from uncertainty in the physical climate response.

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Do not collapse unlike uncertainties
sections.body: A sound revision treats Scenario L versus H as conditional human-choice inputs and treats cloud response as part of physical or structural model uncertainty. Neither source of spread means the projections carry no information.

sections.title: APPLY — A model that passes one test and misses another
sections.body: A fictional regional model is evaluated on held-out data. Lower absolute error indicates closer agreement.

data.provenance: Manuel Academy fictional evaluation dataset constructed for model-critique practice.
data.limit: Aggregate error does not show spatial bias, extremes, trend timing, or causal correctness.

sections.title: APPLY — Write a calibrated model evaluation

items.prompt: Evaluate whether this model is fit for a summer-water-planning decision. Use all three metrics, identify the decision-relevant weakness, and name one additional evaluation needed.

sections.title: FEEDBACK — Fitness depends on the decision
sections.body: Temperature and pressure meet their predeclared thresholds, but summer precipitation misses the threshold and is directly relevant to water planning. A calibrated conclusion can reject this use without claiming the model is useless for every purpose. Spatial bias, extremes, and independent precipitation tests would strengthen the evaluation.

sections.title: WHAT YOU LEARNED
sections.body: Climate projections are conditional ranges from evaluated physical models. Uncertainty has identifiable sources and does not erase evidence.

sections.title: EVIDENCE YOU USED
sections.body: You used hindcast ranges, held-out evaluation metrics, scenario intervals, model structure, and stated limitations.

sections.title: HOW YOU DID
sections.body: Your saved uncertainty revision and fit-for-purpose evaluation provide disciplinary evidence. They remain pending assessment; viewing a projection is not mastery.

sections.title: WHAT TO PRACTICE
sections.body: Practice matching model-validation evidence to the variable, scale, and decision being evaluated.

items.prompt: Explain why a validated hindcast and a quantified projection range strengthen a climate claim without proving one exact future outcome.

sections.title: COURSE PROGRESS
sections.body: This isolated sample does not change your course record. In a released lesson, assessed independent evidence is required before progress or mastery changes.
